Research Approaches & Designs

Research designs — experimental, quasi-experimental, descriptive, correlational, qualitative and their threats to validity.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Describe quantitative designs
  • Explain experimental and quasi-experimental designs
  • Describe qualitative and mixed designs
  • Identify threats to validity

In simple words

The design is the plan for answerng the research question. It decides how data are collected and how trustworthy the conclusions are.

Quantitative designs

Design What it does
Descriptive Describes what exists
Correlational Tests relationships between variables
Cross-sectional Data at one point of time
Longitudinal Data over time
Case study Deep study of one case
Comparative Compares two or more groups

Experimental designs

Design Description
True experimental Randomisation, control group, intervention, measurement
Quasi-experimental Intervention without randomisation
Pre-test / post-test control group Measures before and after the intervention
Solomon four-group Controls for the testing effect

Elements: manipulation, control, randomisation, measurement.

Qualitative designs

  • Phenomenology — lived experience
  • Grounded theory — builds theory from data
  • Ethnography — culture of a group
  • Case study — a case in depth
  • Historical research — past records

Threats to validity

Threat Effect
History Outside events change the result
Maturation Natural change over time
Testing effect Repeating the test changes results
Instrument change Tool or observer changes
Selection bias Groups differ at the start
Attrition Participants dropping out
Maturation Participants grow tired

🔴 Design decides how much you can claim

A descriptive study can say “this is the situation”. Only an experimental study with control can say the intervention caused the change.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Descriptive designs describe; correlational designs test relationships.
  2. True experimental designs use randomisation, control and manipulation.
  3. Quasi-experimental designs lack randomisation.
  4. Threats include history, maturation, testing and selection.
  5. Qualitative designs explore meaning and experience.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Longitudinal designs follow the same subjects over time.
  2. Case study gives depth, not generalisation.
  3. Ethnography studies culture.
  4. Piloting tests the tool before the study.
  5. Blinding reduces observer bias.

📌 Memory trick

Experimental elements: M-C-R-M — Manipulate, Control, Randomise, Measure.

60-second revision

  • Designs: descriptive, correlational, experimental, quasi-experimental.
  • True experiments randomise and control; quasi-experiments do not.
  • Pre-test and post-test with control group is common in nursing.
  • Qualitative designs explore meaning.
  • History, maturation, testing, selection and attrition threaten validity.

Test yourself

Which design can show cause and effect?

Answer: C. Only true experimental designs with randomisation and control can support cause and effect.

A quasi-experimental design lacks:

Answer: B. Quasi-experimental designs use an intervention and measurement but lack randomisation.

Natural improvement in patients over time is a threat called:

Answer: B. Maturation is natural change within participants over the study period.

Ethnography is used to study:

Answer: B. Ethnography examines the culture and practices of a defined group.

A pre-test and post-test control group design uses:

Answer: B. Both groups are measured before and after, allowing comparison of the change.
